text: Incident Management starts with one table. The incident table extends task, the same parent table behind problem, change, and request item — which is why incident already arrives with fields like short description, state, priority, and assignment group built in, instead of each ITSM application defining them from scratch.

System Administration's table hierarchy lesson showed you this inheritance in the abstract. Here it means incident, problem, change, and request item all share one set of core fields, defined once at the task level — security rules and the numbering scheme ServiceNow uses for records are solved once there too, instead of every ITSM app reinventing them separately.

Out of the box, incident carries six real state values: New, In Progress, On Hold, Resolved, Closed, and Canceled. ITSM Foundations covered these as ITIL concepts. Implementing Incident Management means deciding which transitions between those states the platform should actually allow, and which it should block, rather than leaving every transition wide open.

On Hold is not just a state flip. A correctly implemented instance requires a real Hold Reason the moment State is set to On Hold — Awaiting Caller, Awaiting Change, or Awaiting Vendor — so a manager's dashboard can answer what tickets are actually waiting on, not just how many are stuck with no explanation at all.

A Data Policy, conditioned on State equals Resolved, makes Resolution Code and Close Notes mandatory only at that point in the lifecycle — not on every record, in every state, all the time. And a mature instance blocks the jump straight from New to Closed, because Resolved is where the resolution evidence actually lives, and skipping it loses that record permanently.

Table inheritance, a real six-state model, a required Hold Reason, and a Data Policy that enforces resolution evidence before closure. Next up: Priority, Impact, and Urgency — and the real mechanism that calculates Priority automatically instead of leaving it a manual, inconsistent field.
